assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstrations of record stability and accuracy with strontium, redefined what can be measured. They moved timekeeping to the 10^-18 regime, opened tests of relativity and variation of constants, and enabled relativistic geodesy. This is a clear, original and highly durable measurement advance, which fits my view that knowledge is limited by what we can measure and how accurately.
assessment.attribution: Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength lattice idea and Ye's JILA realisation and systematic-uncertainty work are the two decisive strands, and the credited list has exactly these two. A two-person prize is clean. Other groups (for example Lemonde, Bloom, Hinkley) contributed but are not credited. Ye overlaps with the Hall-lab environment I have personal links to, and I would flag that as a potential connection.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed by many national laboratories at 10^-18, and the redefinition of the second is under discussion. Hall and Hänsch were recognised in 2005 for the comb, and this is the natural successor, so timing is good.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution of other lattice-clock groups and of single-ion clocks should affect how credit is shaped is unresolved.
I have not independently verified the exact current accuracy records.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices turned Hubbard-type models into controllable laboratory systems, with the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, single-site imaging and quantum gas microscopes. It is conceptually original, widely adopted and links atomic physics to condensed-matter and many-body questions.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch supplied the theoretical proposal, Greiner and Bloch demonstrated the Mott transition, and Bloch and Greiner developed microscope-level control. Five names are credited, and the field has strong contributions from Esslinger (fermions) and Cirac. I choose Zoller (theory), Bloch and Greiner (experiment), but Esslinger and Jaksch (not credited) make the allocation contestable.
assessment.maturity: The platform is mature and replicated worldwide, with tens of groups producing results. Timeliness is good, though the BEC prize of 2001 and Zoller's overlap with other candidates may argue for staggering.
uncertainties: Allocation among five credited names is not obviously clean.
Whether the prize should reward the platform or specific simulation results is unsettled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution turned fundamental quantum properties, no-cloning and entanglement, into a protocol for secure communication. BB84 and Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based scheme are original and conceptually clean, and they are realised in fibre and satellite links. The 2022 prize on Bell tests makes the area contiguous to recent recognition.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) and Ekert (E91) are the core theory contributors, and this is a natural three-person configuration. Jian-Wei Pan led the main experimental demonstrations but would make four, so the proposed set leaves experiment out and the credit question would need discussion.
assessment.maturity: Protocols are decades old and field experiments are confirmed independently, but practical security against implementation attacks and the commercial role remain evolving. Recognition of the theory is arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether QKD's physical impact is large enough relative to other quantum-information topics is debatable.
Exclusion of Pan's experimental contributions and of Wiesner's earlier idea is a real attribution risk.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators created a new classification of electronic phases and a theory-experiment success: Kane and Mele's prediction, Molenkamp's HgTe observation and the 3D materials. Impact on condensed-matter physics is very large and the discovery is clear and original.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele (theory, Z2 invariant) with Molenkamp (first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells, following Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction) form a coherent set. Hasan's 3D realisation is credited but left out, and Bernevig, Zhang and Moore/Balents are not credited at all, so allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent groups over nearly two decades and material-specific interpretations are stable. Technological applications are still limited, but scientific recognition is mature.
uncertainties: Competing claims between 2D and 3D realisations and the omission of Zhang and Bernevig.
This is outside my own specialty, so I rely on general knowledge of the field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene combined a precise flat-band prediction with the observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle in 2018. It opened the moiré field, which is now a major platform for tunable quantum matter.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the magic angle in 2011, and Jarillo-Herrero's group delivered the decisive 2018 experiments. Andrei's earlier STM evidence of flat bands is credited and a real competing claim, and Cao, the first author of the 2018 papers, is not credited.
assessment.maturity: Replicated widely, but the origin of superconductivity is not settled and the field is still developing, so it may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Credit among Andrei, Jarillo-Herrero and the theory pair is open and may need all four, exceeding the three-person limit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single defect spins, especially NV centres in diamond, allowed room-temperature quantum sensing at the nanoscale and solid-state qubits. This matches my interest in precision measurement and optical addressing of spins in crystals.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup demonstrated single NV optical detection in 1997, Awschalom drove coherent control and the broader defect-spin programme, and Lukin led nanoscale sensing and quantum registers. Walsworth is credited as well, and the leading contributions are spread over four people, so the choice of three is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Widely replicated, with applications in biology and materials. Some applications are still maturing, and the discovery is diffuse rather than a single event.
uncertainties: The discovery is a family of results rather than a single crisp finding.
Allocation among four credited names is not clear-cut.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for trapped-ion quantum gates and the experimental implementation of quantum computation and simulation with ions are original and well validated. The field follows the 2012 recognition of Wineland for ion control, which reduces novelty of the control aspect.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller provided the 1995 proposal and Blatt is a leading experimentalist, though Wineland's group did first gates and Monroe, Häffner and others made major contributions. Zoller also appears in other candidates, which may constrain a coherent overall prize allocation.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed, and commercial systems exist, but the overlap with the 2012 prize and ongoing scaling work make the timing less pressing.
uncertainties: Overlap with Wineland's 2012 recognition and with Zoller's other candidacy.
Omitted experimentalists such as Monroe and Wineland's group.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry provides inertial and gravitational measurements of exceptional precision and tests of fundamental physics. This falls squarely in precision measurement with matter waves and is a natural extension of laser cooling honoured in 1997.
assessment.attribution: Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich are plausible pioneers, but the credit is spread over Chu, Chu's group, Kasevich-Chu, Mlynek, Keith and others, so the prize configuration is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Well established as a technique, but flagship results such as gravitational-wave detectors and equivalence-principle tests are still in development.
uncertainties: Its scientific impact beyond metrology is still being demonstrated.
